title: Orchard and Regiment
premise: In the waning years of a border war, Kestrel Okafor, apprentice to a mapmaker who died protecting his masterwork, inherits an unfinished atlas and the ledger of names it contains — a record of every family the occupying army displaced to requisition their orchards. When the army seizes the town and the ledger itself, Kestrel realizes the names are both evidence and death warrant: the armistice negotiators will need proof of the requisitions, but the colonel who ordered them needs the ledger burned. Over nine days, she smuggles the atlas page by page past three checkpoints, disguised as survey work, guided by a deserter who once signed the orders. At the third checkpoint, with the armistice hours from signature, Kestrel must choose between the atlas — her master's legacy and her own identity as his heir — and the deserter's life, and she finds a third way: she testifies, mapping the town's losses aloud in the negotiators' tent, and the atlas enters the record under both their names.
about_author: Oscar Delacroix is the pen name of a former cartographic archivist who spent a decade cataloguing requisitioned property records from forgotten border wars. Orchard and Regiment is his second novel, written in a farmhouse that once appeared, unnamed, on a military survey map.

chapters.title: The Weight of Ink
chapters.summary: Kestrel finishes inking the final coastal plate of her dead master's atlas while the town below harvests its orchards early, fearing the war's end will bring confiscation rather than peace. When army riders post requisition notices, she hides the ledger of displaced names inside the atlas's binding. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: grief braided with quiet defiance — she measures the world in what can be carried.

chapters.title: Requisition at Dawn
chapters.summary: Soldiers occupy the town square and confiscate the survey office, seizing the ledger with all the names. The requisitioning colonel, Verrec, recognizes Kestrel's master's work and conscripts her to redraw the orchard boundaries for army supply routes. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: humiliation curdling into resolve as she sees her craft weaponized against the very people the atlas was meant to honor.

chapters.title: What the Colonel Keeps
chapters.summary: Working under guard in the commandeered office, Kestrel discovers Verrec has kept the ledger intact rather than burning it — leverage, she realizes, for his own survival after the armistice. She copies the first hidden page onto tracing paper during a night shift. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: the cold clarity of understanding that everyone, even her enemy, is bargaining for what they can carry.

chapters.title: The Deserter's Map
chapters.summary: A wounded deserter, Ilan Sere, takes shelter in the orchard cold cellar where Kestrel caches her tracings; she recognizes him as the junior officer whose signature appears on the original requisition orders. Instead of denouncing him, she bargains: he knows the checkpoint protocols, and she needs to move pages. POV: Kestrel, with a brief Ilan interlude. Emotional beat: wary, transactional trust between two people complicit in different ways.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Bridge
chapters.summary: Kestrel walks the first checkpoint carrying tracings sewn into a surveyor's satchel, bluffing her way past a sergeant who knew her master, while Ilan creates a diversion downstream. She passes — but the sergeant reports her route to Verrec. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: the vertigo of success that feels like exposure; the price of survival is being seen.

chapters.title: Orchards as Evidence
chapters.summary: Verrec confronts Kestrel obliquely, testing her loyalty by asking her to authenticate a forged map that would erase a massacred village. She complies outwardly, then realizes forgery cuts both ways: she can alter the army's own survey to corroborate the ledger. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: a dangerous awakening — her inheritance is not just the atlas but the power of the map itself.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Orchard Line
chapters.summary: With the army's doctored survey as cover, Kestrel and Ilan move the bulk of the ledger through the second checkpoint hidden in requisitioned cider barrels. The plan frays when a soldier recognizes Ilan; he lets himself be detained so the barrels pass. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: guilt and gratitude entangled — she has the evidence and has spent another person to keep it.

chapters.title: Armistice Weather
chapters.summary: Negotiators arrive at the garrison town; rumors say the armistice may be signed without any accounting of requisitions, making the ledger worthless — or the only thing that matters. Verrec, cornered by his own superiors, decides to burn it. Kestrel learns the burning is set for the night before signature. POV: Kestrel, with Verrec's private reckoning. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into a deadline; every theme converges on a single night.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Burning
chapters.summary: Climax. Kestrel infiltrates the garrison during the ledger's burning and saves only the final signature page, then walks it past the third checkpoint — the negotiators' own gate — by claiming the right of testimony. Ilan, released under amnesty rumor, vouches for her at the cost of his own pardon. She enters the tent as the pens are being dipped. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into authorship — she stops smuggling the past and starts dictating it.

chapters.title: The Atlas, Finished
chapters.summary: In the negotiators' tent, Kestrel reads the names aloud and maps the requisitions from memory, her testimony written into the armistice annex. The atlas is completed under two names — her master's and her own — and the orchards are ordered restored, though many families will not return. Kestrel stays to draw the town as it was. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: bittersweet inheritance — survival has a price, and identity is what remains when everything else is carried away.
